stages.title: Asking questions
stages.hook: Why is the sky blue? Why do cats purr? What is one question you can ask about a leaf?
explain: A question is a way to find out more. Questions often start with who, what, where, when, why or how.
Good thinkers ask lots of questions. Asking is how we learn new things. It is fine not to know. Not knowing is where learning starts.
You can ask a question, then look, listen, or ask a helper to find the answer. Some questions can be checked, like "How tall is the door?"

example.q: You see a puddle that was not there yesterday. What question could you ask?
steps: Think about what you see.
Pick a starting word, like why or where.
Make it a question.
example.a: Where did the puddle come from?

analogies.home: You see a new plant in the kitchen. You ask, "What is it called?" and a grown-up tells you.
analogies.farm: A farmer sees a hen that is not eating. She asks, "Why is she not hungry?"
analogies.nature: You see a snail on a wall. You ask, "Where is it going?"

stages.mnemonic: Who, what, where, when, why, how: six helpers that ask for you.
terms: Words we ask to find out something.
What we learn when we find out.

misc.wrong: Asking questions means you are not clever.
misc.right: Asking questions is what clever people do. It is how everyone learns.

trip.prompt: Look for a thing in the pictures that makes you ask "why?"

questions.q: Which one is a question?
o: I like the moon a lot.
questions.why: A question asks to find out something, and it ends with a question mark.

questions.q: Which word can start a question?
questions.why: Why, what, who, where, when and how all start questions.

questions.q: You do not know how a bird flies. What is a good thing to do?
questions.why: Asking is the best first step when you want to know something.

questions.q: Mia sees a seed in the soil. Which is the best question?
o: What will the seed grow into?
The seed is brown and small.
questions.why: The question is about the seed and asks to find out something.

questions.q: What is an answer?
questions.why: An answer is what we learn when we find out.

questions.q: Is it okay to say "I do not know"?
o: Yes, then we can ask and learn
questions.why: Everyone does not know many things. Saying so is the start of learning.

questions.q: Which question can you check by looking?
o: What is a star made of far away?
What will happen in a year?
questions.why: You can look at the door and see its colour.

questions.q: Put these in order: ask, find out, notice something new.
questions.why: First you notice, then you ask, then you find out.

questions.q: Match the starting word to what it asks about.
questions.why: Who asks about people, where about places and when about time.

questions.q: Kofi asks, "Why do ants walk in a line?" What is he being?
questions.why: Wanting to know more is being curious.

panel.q: Why is a question like "How tall is the door?" easier to answer than "What is the best colour?"
o: Colours are never nice to see
Questions with more words are harder
panel.why: You can check a height with a ruler. A best colour is just a liking.

panel.q: Ana asks a lot of questions and feels silly. What should she know?
panel.why: Questions are how we learn. Good thinkers ask many.

panel.q: Which question will help you most to find out why a plant is drooping?
o: Is it a plant or a tree?
panel.why: A question that can be tested helps you find the cause.

teach.model: Asking questions helps us find out things. Questions start with words like who, what, why. We can look, listen or ask a helper to find the answer. Not knowing is a good place to start.

points.ask: How do I ask about something?
How do I get the answer?

stages.title: Observing carefully
stages.hook: Can you spot five things in your room that are round? Look closely!
explain: Observing means looking very carefully. We use our eyes, ears, nose, hands and tongue. These are our five senses.
Look at one thing for a long time. What colour is it? How big is it? What shape? How does it feel? What does it sound like?
Careful looking helps us find out true things. Fast looking can miss small things, like a tiny bug on a leaf.

example.q: Look at an orange. What can you tell about it?
steps: Use your eyes: it is round and orange.
Use your hands: it is bumpy.
Use your nose: it smells sweet.
example.a: It is round, orange, bumpy and smells sweet.

analogies.home: You look at your shoe. You see the laces, the colour and a small hole.
analogies.farm: A farmer looks at a cow. She sees if its eyes are bright and if it is walking well.
analogies.nature: You watch a spider. You see eight legs and a thin thread.

stages.mnemonic: Eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands: five helpers for looking at the land.
terms: To look and notice with care.
Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching.

misc.wrong: If I look once, I have seen everything.
misc.right: Looking again often shows new things. Careful observers look more than once.

stages.limits: Our senses can be fooled, so we look or feel again to check.

trip.prompt: Find a picture that shows you can use more than one sense.

questions.q: How many senses do we usually name?
questions.why: Sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch make five.

questions.q: Which sense do you use to hear a bell?
questions.why: Ears are for hearing.

questions.q: You want to know if a rock is smooth. What do you use?
questions.why: Your hands can feel smooth or rough.

questions.q: You want to know the colour of a kite. What do you use?
questions.why: Colours are seen with your eyes.

questions.q: Which is a careful observation?
o: The leaf has three points and is green
Leaves are boring to look at
I think the leaf is nice
questions.why: It tells true details we can see.

questions.q: Lola looks at a flower for a long time and sees a small bee. Why did she see it?
questions.why: Looking carefully helps us notice small things.

questions.q: A cake smells sweet. Which sense found that?
questions.why: The nose smells things.

questions.q: Match the sense to the body part.
questions.why: Each sense has its own helper.

questions.q: You see 3 birds on a wall. Then 2 more come. How many birds do you see now?
questions.why: 3 + 2 = 5. Counting is a kind of careful looking.

questions.q: A cat is hiding in the grass. How can you find it?
questions.why: Slow, careful looking helps you spot hidden things.

panel.q: Why can two people see the same picture and notice different things?
panel.why: Each person may notice other parts. Looking again helps us see more.

panel.q: Sam says the water is cold. How could he be more careful?
o: Use a thermometer or touch it again
panel.why: Checking again or using a tool gives better information.

panel.q: Which is an observation, not an opinion?
panel.why: Red can be seen by anyone. The others are opinions.

teach.model: To observe means to look with care. We use our five senses: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching. We look for colour, shape, size and feel. We look more than once, so we do not miss small things.

points.ask: What do I do to observe?
How do I do it well?

stages.title: Identifying similarities and differences
stages.hook: A cat and a dog. How are they the same? How are they different?
explain: Things can be the same in some ways and different in others. A cat and a dog both have fur and four legs. A cat meows. A dog barks.
To compare, pick one thing to look at, such as size, colour or sound. Then ask: same or different?
Finding same and different helps us sort things and understand them. It is the start of big ideas in science and maths.

example.q: How are an apple and a banana the same and different?
steps: Same: both are fruit, both can be eaten.
Different: one is round and red or green, one is long and yellow.
example.a: Same: fruit. Different: shape and colour.

analogies.home: A spoon and a fork are the same: both help us eat. They are different: a fork has points.
analogies.sea: A fish and a whale both live in water. A whale breathes air and a fish uses gills.
analogies.nature: A rose and a daisy are both flowers. They have different petals.

stages.mnemonic: Same and different: two friends, one pair.
terms: Look at two things to find same and different.

misc.wrong: If two things are the same in one way, they are the same in every way.
misc.right: Two things can be the same in one way and different in another. A whale and a fish both swim, but a whale breathes air.

trip.prompt: Look at the animals in the pictures. Find two that are alike and one that is different.

questions.q: A ball and a coin are both round. Are they the same in every way?
o: No, they differ in size and use
Yes, they are the same always
Yes, you can eat them both
No, a coin is not round
questions.why: Same in one way (round) does not mean same in every way.

questions.q: Which two are the same kind of thing?
questions.why: Dogs and cats are both animals.

questions.q: How is a bird different from a fish?
o: A bird can fly with wings
A fish can fly with wings
A bird has gills for water
A fish has feathers on it
questions.why: Birds have wings and feathers. Fish have fins and gills.

questions.q: What does "compare" mean?
questions.why: To compare is to look at things to see how they are alike and unlike.

questions.q: Look: red cube, red ball, blue cube. Which two are the same shape?
questions.why: Both are cubes.

questions.q: Look: red cube, red ball, blue cube. Which two are the same colour?
questions.why: Both are red.

questions.q: Which is a difference between day and night?
o: The sky is light in the day
Both have the same bright light
Night has the sun up high
Day has only the moon out
questions.why: In the day the sun makes the sky light.

questions.q: Match each pair to one way they are the same.
questions.why: Each pair shares one thing.

questions.q: Put the steps in order for comparing two toys.
items: Look at one feature like colour
questions.why: Choose, pick a feature, then say.

questions.q: Why do we compare things?
o: To learn how they are alike and unlike
To make a lot of noise
questions.why: Comparing helps us understand and sort things.

panel.q: A zebra and a horse both have four legs and a tail. Does it mean they are the same animal?
o: No, they differ in other ways like stripes
Yes, they are the same animal
No, horses have no tails at all
panel.why: Sharing some features does not make things the same.

panel.q: Why should we pick one feature when comparing?
o: It is a rule about noise
panel.why: Looking at one feature at a time helps us avoid mixing things up.

panel.q: Two shapes are both red. Which sentence is true?
o: They match in colour, and may differ in shape
They are not alike at all
They are the very same shape
panel.why: Matching in one feature does not tell us about the others.

teach.model: To compare means to look at two things and find how they are the same and how they are different. We pick one feature, like colour or size, and check each thing. Two things can be alike in one way and not in another.

points.ask: What do I look for first?
What else do I look for?

stages.title: Recognising patterns
stages.hook: Clap, clap, stomp. Clap, clap, stomp. What do you do next?
explain: A pattern is something that repeats. Red, blue, red, blue is a pattern. Clap, clap, stomp, clap, clap, stomp is a pattern too.
The part that repeats is called the unit. In red, blue, red, blue the unit is red, blue.
Patterns are everywhere: stripes, tiles, songs, days of the week. When we see a pattern, we can guess what comes next.

example.q: What comes next? Red, blue, red, blue, red, ?
steps: Find the part that repeats: red, blue.
We have just had red.
So blue comes next.

analogies.music: A drum beat goes boom, tap, boom, tap. The pattern helps you dance.
analogies.home: Tiles on the floor go black, white, black, white.
analogies.nature: Day, night, day, night: the sky follows a pattern.

stages.mnemonic: A pattern is a song that says its own words again and again.
terms: Something that repeats in a way we can predict.

misc.right: A pattern can be made of sounds, numbers, shapes or movements.

trip.prompt: Look for patterns in the pictures, such as stripes or spots.

questions.q: What comes next? Circle, square, circle, square, circle, ?
questions.why: The unit is circle, square, so square is next.

questions.q: What comes next? Clap, stomp, clap, stomp, clap, ?
questions.why: The unit is clap, stomp.

questions.q: What number comes next? 2, 4, 6, 8, ?
questions.why: The numbers go up by 2 each time. 8 + 2 = 10.

questions.q: What is a pattern?
questions.why: A pattern repeats in a way we can predict.

questions.q: Which is a pattern?
o: Red, red, blue, red, red, blue
Red, blue, green, pink, grey, white
questions.why: Red, red, blue repeats.

questions.q: Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, ? What comes next?
questions.why: Days of the week repeat, and Sunday comes after Saturday.

questions.q: Pattern: star, moon, moon, star, moon, moon, star. What comes next?
questions.why: The unit is star, moon, moon. After star comes moon.

questions.q: Why are patterns useful?
o: We can guess what comes next
They are only for art class
questions.why: Seeing a pattern lets us predict.

questions.q: Put these days in order.
questions.why: The days of the week follow a pattern in this order.

questions.q: Match the pattern to its repeating unit.
pairs: A B A B A B
Red Blue Blue Red Blue Blue
questions.why: Find the part that repeats.

panel.q: A pattern goes 1, 3, 5, 7. Which number comes next?
panel.why: It goes up by 2 each time. 7 + 2 = 9.

panel.q: Dan says a pattern must repeat exactly. Which pattern breaks his rule but is still a pattern?
o: A page with nothing on it
panel.why: Number patterns can grow by the same step instead of repeating.

panel.q: Why can a pattern help a farmer?
o: Seasons repeat so he can plan
panel.why: Seasons come in a pattern, which helps plan planting.

teach.model: A pattern is something that repeats. It has a part that comes again and again, called the unit. When we find the unit, we can guess what comes next. We can find patterns in colours, sounds, numbers and days.

stages.title: Sorting and classifying objects
stages.hook: You have a big pile of toys. How can you tidy them so you can find things fast?
explain: Sorting means putting things in groups. All the red blocks go together. All the cars go together.
To sort, we choose a rule. The rule could be colour, size, shape or what it is for. Every item must follow the rule.
The same things can be sorted in different ways. A red ball and a blue ball could go together for shape, or the red ball with a red car for colour.

example.q: Sort these: apple, banana, carrot, cherry. Which are fruit?
steps: The rule is: is it a fruit?
Apple: yes. Banana: yes. Carrot: no. Cherry: yes.
example.a: Fruit: apple, banana, cherry. Not fruit: carrot.

analogies.home: You put spoons in one drawer and plates in another.
analogies.city: A shop puts fruit on one shelf and bread on another.
analogies.farm: A farmer puts eggs in one box and milk in another.

stages.mnemonic: Sort with a rule, one by one, and every group is done.
terms: A set of things that share something.
What we use to decide which group.

misc.wrong: There is only one way to sort things.
misc.right: You can sort the same things in many ways, using different rules.

trip.prompt: Find a picture that shows animals grouped. What is the rule?

questions.q: You sort buttons by colour. Which belong together?
o: A blue and a red button
A big and a small button
questions.why: The rule is colour, so same colour goes together.

questions.q: What do we need to sort?
questions.why: A rule tells us which group each thing goes in.

questions.q: Dog, cat, cow, car. Which one does not belong with animals?
questions.why: A car is not an animal.

questions.q: Where would a spoon go?
questions.why: Spoons, forks and knives are for eating.

questions.q: Red ball, blue ball, red cube. Sort by shape. Which go together?
questions.why: Both are balls.

questions.q: Red ball, blue ball, red cube. Sort by colour. Which go together?
questions.why: Both are red.

questions.q: Why is sorting helpful?
o: It is a very loud game
questions.why: Groups make things easy to find.

questions.q: You have 3 red cars and 4 blue cars. How many cars in all?
Match each thing to its group.
questions.why: Each belongs to a natural group.

questions.q: Can the same toys be sorted in two ways?
questions.why: Different rules make different groups.

panel.q: A leaf is green and small. Which group could it go into?
panel.why: The group depends on which rule you choose.

panel.q: Why must every item in a group follow the rule?
o: To make the page look long
Just for fun and nothing else
panel.why: A clear rule keeps groups useful.

panel.q: A shop puts all tools in one place. What is the sorting rule?
panel.why: Tools are grouped by use.

teach.model: Sorting means putting things in groups. First pick a rule, like colour or what it is for. Then put each thing in the group that fits. You can sort the same things in a new way with a new rule.

stages.title: Simple cause and effect
stages.hook: What happens to a puddle when the sun shines on it all day?
explain: A cause is why something happens. An effect is what happens. If you drop a ball, it falls. The drop is the cause. The fall is the effect.
Effects have causes. If the grass is wet, a cause might be rain. But careful: it could be something else, like a sprinkler.
Finding causes helps us fix problems and make good plans. Always ask: what made this happen?

example.q: The plant is drooping. You water it, and it stands up. What was the cause?
steps: The effect: the plant stood up.
Before that, you watered it.
So water was the cause.
example.a: The water made the plant stand up.

analogies.home: You flip the switch. The light comes on. Flipping is the cause.
analogies.nature: The sun shines. The snow melts. Sunshine is the cause.
analogies.farm: The farmer feeds the hens. They come running.

stages.mnemonic: Cause pushes the domino. Effect is the domino that falls.
terms: What happens because of the cause.
A word that links effect and cause.

misc.wrong: If one thing happens before another, it always caused it.
misc.right: Sometimes two things just happen near each other. We must check.

trip.prompt: Find a picture in which one thing makes another thing happen.

questions.q: You push a toy car and it rolls. What is the cause?
questions.why: The push made it roll.

questions.q: The ice cream melted. What is the best cause?
o: It was in the hot sun
questions.why: Heat melts ice cream.

questions.q: What is an effect?
o: A type of fruit to eat
questions.why: An effect is the result.

questions.q: You drop a glass and it breaks. What is the effect?
questions.why: The break is the result.

questions.q: You wear a coat because...
questions.why: Cold weather is the cause.

questions.q: The class is quiet. Which is a possible cause?
o: The teacher is reading a story
questions.why: A story can make a class listen quietly.

questions.q: Put in order: the plant grows, you plant a seed, you water the seed.
questions.why: Seed, then water, then growth.

questions.q: Match each cause to its effect.
questions.why: Each cause leads to an effect.

questions.q: Tia went out, and then it rained. Did Tia make it rain?
o: Yes, because she went out first
questions.why: Happening first does not mean it caused it.

questions.q: A seed needs 2 days to sprout. How many days for 3 seeds planted together?
questions.why: They grow at the same time, so the time is still 2 days.

panel.q: The street is wet. Is rain the only possible cause?
o: No, a hose or a sprinkler could do it
panel.why: There can be more than one possible cause.

panel.q: Why is it good to know a cause?
panel.why: Knowing the cause helps us change the result.

panel.q: The light does not come on. Which check helps find the cause?
o: Is it plugged in and is the bulb working?
panel.why: We test likely causes one by one.

teach.model: A cause is why something happens. An effect is what happens next. If you flip the switch, the light comes on. Flipping is the cause. Light is the effect. We can use "because" to join them.

stages.title: Making predictions
stages.hook: You see dark clouds. What do you think will happen next?
explain: A prediction is a good guess about what will happen. It uses clues. Dark clouds are a clue that rain may come.
A good guess is not the same as a sure thing. We can be wrong. If we are wrong, we learn and guess better next time.
To predict, look for clues, think about what happened before, and then say what you think. Afterwards, check: were you right?

example.q: A ball is at the top of a slope. Predict what will happen.
steps: Clue: slopes go down.
Clue: balls roll.
So the ball will roll down.

analogies.nature: Dark clouds are a clue that rain may come.
analogies.farm: The hens go to bed at dusk. A farmer predicts they will be in the coop soon.
analogies.sport: A runner sees a ball coming and guesses where it will land.

stages.mnemonic: Clue, think, guess, check: four steps, never a wreck.
terms: Say what you think will happen.
A fact that helps you guess.
Look to see if you were right.

misc.wrong: A prediction must always be right.
misc.right: A prediction is a good guess. We check it and learn.

trip.prompt: Find the weather clues on the page.

questions.q: What is a prediction?
o: A good guess about what will happen
questions.why: We predict what may happen next.

questions.q: What helps you make a good prediction?
questions.why: Clues from what we see and know help us guess well.

questions.q: Lots of dark clouds. What might you predict?
o: It will snow in the desert
It will be a rainbow only
questions.why: Dark clouds are a clue for rain.

questions.q: You mix blue and yellow paint. What do you predict?
questions.why: Blue and yellow make green.

questions.q: You were wrong about a prediction. What is best?
questions.why: Being wrong teaches us to think better.

questions.q: A bell rings at school every day at lunch. It is almost lunch. What do you predict?
questions.why: The past pattern is a clue.

questions.q: Put the prediction steps in order.
questions.why: Clues first, then guess, then check.

questions.q: You put a seed in soil. It takes 5 days to sprout. If you plant on day 1, on which day do you predict it will sprout? (Day 1 plus 5 days)
questions.why: Day 1 + 5 days = day 6.

questions.q: Match the clue to the prediction.
questions.why: Each clue points to a likely result.

questions.q: Why do we check a prediction?
o: To see if we were right
questions.why: Checking shows how good our guess was.

panel.q: You predict it will rain, but it stays dry. What does this show?
panel.why: Predictions are guesses, not sure facts.

panel.q: Which prediction has better clues?
o: It is winter and snow is falling, so it will be cold
I like blue so it will be cold
My toy says it will be cold
I have no clue at all
panel.why: Good predictions use real clues.

panel.q: Why does checking your prediction make you a better thinker?
o: It is a rule to follow
panel.why: Checking lets you improve your clues next time.

teach.model: To predict means to make a good guess about what will happen. First look for clues. Then think about what happened before. Then say your guess. After, check if you were right.

points.ask: What do I do with the clues?
What do I do at the end?

stages.title: Solving elementary puzzles
stages.hook: A box has 4 sides in the same size. Can you work out the shape?
explain: A puzzle is a problem that makes you think. You can solve it with a plan. Many puzzles need you to look, try, and try again.
Try this: look at what you know, make a small guess, test it. If it does not work, try something else. Do not give up.
Puzzles train careful thinking. They also show that there can be more than one way to solve something.

example.q: Ben has 2 socks. He needs 6 socks for 3 people. How many more?
steps: Count what he has: 2.
He needs 6.

analogies.home: A jigsaw puzzle: you look at the colours and try pieces until they fit.
analogies.sport: A team works out how to pass the ball to the player who is free.
analogies.city: A map puzzle: find the shortest path from home to school.

stages.mnemonic: Look, try, fix, win: puzzles begin with a grin.

misc.wrong: If I cannot solve it quickly, I am not good at puzzles.
misc.right: Everyone needs time. Trying again is how we get better.

trip.prompt: Find a puzzle in the pictures and try to solve it.

questions.q: A puzzle is hard. What is a good first step?
questions.why: Start with what you know.

questions.q: You have 5 apples and give away 2. How many are left?
What shape has 3 sides?
questions.why: A triangle has three sides.

questions.q: A riddle: I have hands but cannot clap. What am I?
questions.why: A clock has hands.

questions.q: What do you do if your first try does not work?
questions.why: Another idea may work.

questions.q: A farmer has 3 hens and 4 more come. How many hens?
Which is one way to solve a jigsaw?
o: Match the colours at the edges
questions.why: Matching colours and edges helps.

questions.q: Put these in order for solving a puzzle.
questions.why: Understand first, then try, then check.

questions.q: Match each puzzle to what it asks you to do.
questions.why: Each has its own kind of thinking.

questions.q: Why is it good to check your answer?
o: To be sure it is right
questions.why: Checking catches mistakes.

panel.q: Two children solve a puzzle in different ways. What does this show?
o: There can be more than one good way
Only one way can be right
panel.why: Many puzzles have more than one path.

panel.q: Why is "try again" a good idea?
o: It makes a lot of noise
panel.why: Mistakes show what does not work.

panel.q: Mia has 10 beads and wants 3 groups of 3 with none left over. How many beads does she use?
panel.why: 3 groups of 3 is 9 beads.

teach.model: A puzzle is a problem that makes us think. First look at what you know. Then try an idea. If it does not work, try another. Last, check your answer.

points.ask: How do I know I am done?

stages.title: Learning from mistakes
stages.hook: You spill some juice. What can you do next time so it does not spill?
explain: Everyone makes mistakes. Mistakes are not bad. They show us what to fix and teach us how to do better.
When you make a mistake, stop and look. What went wrong? What can I do next time? Then try again.
It is brave to say, "I got it wrong." Great thinkers, scientists and builders all make mistakes and learn from them.

example.q: Kai builds a tall tower. It falls. What can he learn?
steps: It fell. Why?
The bottom blocks were small.
Next time use a big block at the bottom.
example.a: Use a big block at the bottom.

analogies.home: You spill water. Next time you hold the cup with two hands.
analogies.sport: You miss a goal. You aim at the corner next time.
analogies.music: You play a wrong note. You slow down and try again.

stages.mnemonic: Oops is how learning starts: look, fix, try again with heart.
terms: Something that did not go as planned.
Do it again with what you learned.

misc.wrong: Mistakes mean I am bad at it.
misc.right: Mistakes are how we all learn. Even experts make them.

trip.prompt: Find a person on the page who tried many times.

questions.q: You make a mistake. What is a good thing to do?
questions.why: Looking at the mistake helps us fix it.

questions.q: Why are mistakes useful?
questions.why: We find out what to change.

questions.q: Your tower of blocks fell. What can you try?
questions.why: A wider base is more stable.

questions.q: Ama spells a word wrong. What helps next?
o: Look at the word again and copy it
questions.why: Checking helps us fix the spelling.

questions.q: Who makes mistakes?
questions.why: All people make mistakes.

questions.q: Which is a brave thing to say?
o: I made a mistake. Let me try again.
questions.why: Admitting a mistake helps us learn.

questions.q: Put in order: try again, make a mistake, find out what went wrong.
questions.why: Mistake, then look, then retry.

questions.q: Match each mistake to a fix.
questions.why: Each fix comes from learning.

questions.q: Kai tries a tower 3 times and learns something each time. How many things has he learned?
questions.why: One lesson each time: 3.

questions.q: Why is "yet" a helpful word? "I cannot do it yet."
o: It means I can never learn
questions.why: "Yet" shows learning can happen.

panel.q: Two children get a sum wrong. One checks and fixes it. The other hides it. Who learns more?
panel.why: Checking turns the mistake into learning.

panel.q: Why do scientists test things many times?
panel.why: Repeating helps find errors.

panel.q: Which attitude helps learning most?
o: It is not my fault, ever
panel.why: A try-again attitude keeps learning going.

teach.model: Everyone makes mistakes. A mistake is a clue about what to change. We look at what went wrong, think of a fix, and try again. This is how we get better.

points.ask: What can I do with it?
